notes.meaning: The people of Jerusalem forgot how good God had been to them when they were young, and their rebellion stirred up His anger. Because of this, the Lord promised to bring the consequences of their actions right back onto their own heads. He would not ignore their wicked deeds or let their unfaithfulness go unpunished.

People who used common sayings would soon apply a familiar proverb to Jerusalem: 'Like mother, like daughter.' The city acted just like the pagan peoples who lived in the land before her. Her daily behavior proved that she had adopted the corrupt character of the Canaanite culture around her.

Jerusalem showed the same twisted character as the ancient Hittite and Amorite peoples who held the land earlier. Just like them, the city rejected her true Lord and even sacrificed her own children to false idols. She was spiritually kin to wicked sister cities that hated God in the very same way.

God points to two sister cities: Samaria to the north and Sodom to the south, along with all their smaller towns. Samaria is called the older sister because she was larger and had more people, while Sodom is called the younger sister because she was smaller. Both places were notorious neighbors whose sins had already brought God's punishment.

Jerusalem did not stop at copying the disgusting practices of her sister cities. In a short time, she went even further into evil and became more corrupt than either of them. Because she had God's law and temple, her willful disobedience was far worse than the sins of the heathen.

The Lord made an oath by His own life that even Sodom had never sunk to the depths reached by Jerusalem and her towns. People thought of Sodom as the most wicked place in history, so this statement was meant to stun the hearers. Greater spiritual privileges meant that Jerusalem had far greater guilt when she turned away from God.

God reveals the root sins of Sodom: pride, plenty of food, and lazy comfort, combined with a refusal to help the poor and needy. Having too much and caring too little made her citizens selfish and hard-hearted. These everyday sins opened the door to all their other shameful actions.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern readers argue that Sodom's primary sin was social and economic injustice rather than sexual immorality.

notes.meaning: Sodom's arrogance grew until her people openly carried out detestable practices right before the eyes of the Lord. Because of this bold rebellion, God wiped the city away in judgment, as everyone knew from history. Persistent defiance against God will eventually bring His certain justice.

Samaria, the northern kingdom, had not done half the evil that Jerusalem committed. Jerusalem piled up so many idols and abominations that she made Samaria and Sodom look relatively righteous by comparison. Her shocking unfaithfulness made other wicked places seem mild next to her.

Jerusalem had gladly condemned her sisters for their sins, but now she had to bear her own heavy shame. Because her rebellion was so vile, she made those evil cities look innocent compared to herself. The disgrace she once directed at others was now turned back onto her own head.

God declares that He will restore the fortunes of Sodom and Samaria, and restore Jerusalem right along with them. Jerusalem would not receive special treatment or come first; she would be put on the very same footing as the sisters she looked down upon. Any hope of future blessing rested entirely on God's free mercy, not on Israel's goodness.

Being brought back alongside Sodom and Samaria was meant to humble Jerusalem completely. When those fallen cities saw Jerusalem suffering the same fate, it gave them a bitter comfort to know they were not alone in their ruin. Jerusalem's proud boasting would finally be shattered by her public humiliation.

The Lord promises that Sodom and Samaria will return to their former state, and Jerusalem and her towns will return as well. Just as their ruin was shared, any future restoration would belong to all of them together. This leveled Jerusalem's pride and showed that God alone decides when and how to heal.

During the seasons of her wealth and self-importance, Jerusalem would not even speak Sodom's name out loud. She viewed the destroyed city with pure contempt and thought she was far too holy to ever face a similar fate. Pride kept her from learning the lesson of God's earlier judgment.

Jerusalem's haughtiness lasted only until her own wickedness was stripped bare by God's judgments. Soon, neighboring enemies like Edom and the Philistines looked down on her with deep contempt and mockery. The very scorn she had poured on Sodom was now returned to her by all her neighbors.

The Lord announced that Jerusalem must fully carry the burden of her shameful idolatry and disgusting deeds. God was not being unfairly harsh; the punishment was the exact match for her long rebellion. His word settled the matter with absolute justice.

God promised to treat Jerusalem exactly as she had treated Him. She had despised her sacred oath by breaking the covenant, the formal marriage-like agreement she made with God at Mount Sinai. Because she threw away that sacred bond, she had to face the bitter results of her unfaithfulness.

Right after warning of judgment, God reveals His amazing mercy. Even though the people broke their promises, the Lord remembers the covenant He made with them in their youth and promises to establish an everlasting agreement that will never end. His faithful love gets the final word over their sin.

When God brings back the other nations and gives them to Jerusalem as daughters, the city will remember her past and feel true repentance. This new family bond would not come from Jerusalem's old covenant rules, which kept outsiders away. Instead, it would flow purely from God's free grace welcoming the nations into His family.

The Lord repeats His promise that He Himself will set up this unbreakable covenant with His people. Through this wonderful act of rescue, they will finally know in their hearts that He is the Lord. They will see that He is completely faithful to His promises, even when they were unfaithful.

God explains that when He makes atonement—freely forgiving and covering all their wrongs—His people will be entirely humbled. They will be so overwhelmed by His gracious pardon that they will never again boast, make excuses, or complain about His ways. True forgiveness takes away our pride and fills the heart with quiet gratitude.
